}}'''John Morgan Greene''' (22 September 1928 – 22 October 2007) was an American theoretical physicist and applied mathematician, known for his work on [[soliton]]s and [[plasma physics]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/notices/200604/comm-steele.pdf Steele Prize for Greene, Notices AMS 2006, pdf file] (384&nbsp;kB)</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.towntopics.com/dec0507/obits.html |title=Obituary from Princeton ''Town Topics'' |access-date=2012-03-31 |archive-date=2013-12-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224110015/http://www.towntopics.com/dec0507/obits.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?greenej |title=John Greene Biography from APS |access-date=2012-03-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160302045020/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?greenej |archive-date=2016-03-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[http://scitation.aip.org/content/aip/magazine/physicstoday/article/61/6/10.1063/1.2947657 John Greene Obituary in Physics Today]</ref>

==Education==
After several successes as a high school student in the state mathematical competitions of Kansas, he received a [[Pepsi Cola]] scholarship at [[Caltech]], where he earned a B. S. in 1950. In 1956 he received a PhD from the [[University of Rochester]] in nuclear physics under David Feldman{{citation needed|date=April 2016}} with a thesis entitled "High-Order Corrections to the Nucleon-Nucleon Potential in Change-Symmetric Pseudoscalar Theory."<ref name=mathgene/>

==Career and research==
After  his PhD, he worked at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]] (on "Project Matterhorn"), where he was one of the leading theoretical physicists and remained until 1982. In 1982 he was Senior Technical Advisor in the theory group of [[General Atomics]] and simultaneously adjunct professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]].

He was the author of a series of works with John Johnson and [[Katherine Weimer]] on equilibria and instabilities in [[Tokamak]] and [[Stellarator]] plasmas in [[magnetohydrodynamics]]. With Johnson and Ray Grimm he developed the computer program PEST (Princeton Equilibrium and Stability in Tokamak's Code). With [[Bruno Coppi]] and others he investigated dissipative instabilities in plasmas. With [[Ira B. Bernstein]] and [[Martin Kruskal]] he did research on [[BGK modes]] (nonlinear wave solutions in plasma physics). In the 1970s he worked on Hamiltonian dynamics in chaos theory. In 1979 he published Greene's criterion for the collapse of tori in [[Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Theorem|KAM theory]].

==Awards and honors==
In 1992, he won the [[James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Green&first_nm=John&year=1992|title=1992 James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics Recipient|last=|first=|date=|website=American Physical Society|language=en|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110518052756/http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Green&first_nm=John&year=1992|archive-date=2011-05-18|access-date=2020-02-13}}</ref> He was a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) and a member of the [[American Geophysical Union]].

In 2006, he received the [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] with [[Martin Kruskal]], [[Robert M. Miura]] and [[Clifford S. Gardner]]<ref>“Korteweg-de-Vries equation and generalizations VI: Methods for exact solution“, Comm.Pure Applied Mathematics, vol. 27, 1974, pp. 97-133</ref> for his work on inverse scattering transformations in the theory of solitons.

==Personal life==
He was married from 1956 on and had a daughter and two grandchildren. He died as a consequence of Parkinson's disease. Greene's father was a professor of chemical engineering at Kansas State.
